Creativity and the Erotic Dimensions of the Analytic Field. Dianne Elise. Routledge, 2019. 334 pp.

Tracy Morgan

Tracy Morgan

Tracy Morgan  

In her book Creativity and the Erotic Dimensions of the Analytic Field, Dianne Elise thinks upending thoughts, thoughts which pose eye-opening questions such as: How exactly does heterosexuality ever flower in a girl, who begins life in union with a woman? In a field where we accept the almost loopy idea that perception begins with the mouth, (Spitz, 1955), can we just as easily accept the idea that our first experience of intercourse takes place via a breast, with a woman pleasurably penetrating us orally? What if we thought of psychoanalytic treatments denuded of erotic transference and countertransference as alarmingly incomplete? Might male impenetrability, physically and psychically, lead to a woman's “frigidity? How can we actually attribute triadic relations to the oedipus complex if a mother's sexuality is devalued or insufficiently embraced, leaving the girl without a worthy opponent over whom to triumph as she sprints to its resolution? After spending time swimming in Elise's thoughts, I started to wonder anew whether the goal of “oedipalization” is even realistic for women, and if perhaps Freud was right after all: maybe our superegos are weaker than men's - and hey, is that such a bad thing?

Of Shells and Carapaces: The Emergence and Crumbling of Microcalcifications

Nilofer Kaul PHD

Nilofer Kaul

Email: niloferkaul@gmail.com

Nilofer Kaul   Training and supervising analyst with the Indian Psychoanalytical Society. She has written two books: Plato's Ghost (Karnac, 2021) and Fearful Symmetry (Zubaan, 2023). She is interested in Wilfred Bion, gender, primitive structures, literature, myths, and questions pertaining to the language of psychoanalysis.

This paper widens the metaphor of shells beyond merely a static defense, to include the dynamic activity of psychic calcification. Autistic functioning is explored in the literature and as a part of the analytic encounter, for both patient and analyst. Freud's theories of the contact barrier and the mystical writing pad and Bion's idea of archaic remains are presented and combined to form an active, palimpsestic model of the psyche. In this model, microscopic movements matter. The author presents two challenging cases that illustrate the importance of patience and attention to micromovements when we are alerted to calcification in the here and now of clinical work.

A Dream That Interprets Itself, by Otto Rank. G. C. Richter, Trans., R. Kramer, Ed. Karnac. 2024. 120 pp.

William Sharp

William Sharp

William Sharp  

There is a reason to mark Freud's Interpretation of Dreams (1900) as the birth of psychoanalysis. Dreams really are the “royal road to the unconscious” in a way few other things are. Dreams get a glimpse of mental activity when the external world's influence is at a minimum. Otto Rank's 1910 book, Ein tram, der sich selbst deutet is published in English for the first time and available through Karnac as A Dream that Interprets Itself (2024). It is translated by Gregory Richter and edited with an introduction by Robert Kramer. The book is a mere 86 pages long including endnotes and index, so will be a quick read for many. It provides a dream and the interpretation that traces itself back to the associations and personality of the dreamer, and as such, is an important reference for those interested in dream interpretation in clinical work as well as for those teaching dream interpretation, symbolic communication, and research in psychoanalysis. The dream is unpacked in a meticulous way that shows the importance and power of interpretation in understanding a patient.

In the first part of the dream, the dreamer reports being a governess in a royal palace. She is to lie down on the floor in supplication, but refuses and is beaten by the Queen. A female attendant is then told to take her into the lilac room and the dreamer is surprised that “I wasn't being treated so badly after all; I had been granted the honor of examining this room” (p. 11). 87

Animal Joy: A Book of Laughter and Resuscitation. by Nuar Alsadir. Graywolf Press. 2022. 320 pp.

Tisch Abelow

Tisch Abelow

Tisch Abelow  

Nuar Alsadir's Animal Joy came at a relevant moment for me; a new friend had suggested that I drop both my careers to become a stand-up comedian. My response to this was, “But I hate comedy.” Similarly, when I learned Alsadir, a psychoanalyst, had gone to clown school, I was skeptical. My immediate assumption was that anyone who would go to clown school, anyone who needed to learn to be funny, was probably not funny, and probably not an author I was interested in reading. And more so, my associations with clowns are scary (John Wayne Gacy, Jr!), not amusing.

But upon embarking on Animal Joy, I relearned what psychoanalysts must repeatedly remind ourselves: not to make assumptions. Lucky for me, the content of the book is serious. Alsadir went to clown school not to become a clown, but as research. In line with Freud's notion that it is not more truthful to be serious, a crucial point for Alsadir is that what makes an audience laugh is honesty and authenticity. responseSet.title: With Thanks to George Ernsberger
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

With Thanks to George Ernsberger

Since 1976, when this journal was first published, there has been one consistent, steady and intrepid force, behind the scenes, editing the pages of Modern Psychoanalysis. This person is none other than George Ernsberger. While George has retired from his post on our publication, he remains very much imprinted in the style, format and quality of Modern Psychoanalysis, forever.

George was “wise about analysts, both as writers and as clinicians, from a fairly sophisticated lay perspective.” He was always, as he would modestly phrase it, “reasonably knowing” about the profession, even if his work wasn't the work of a professional analyst. He was primarily interested in writers, and especially young or new writers who were embarking on writing about our body of theory/thought, as applied clinically.

The brilliance and experience George readily shared was a gift, even if he didn't always believe in niceties or sugar coating his thoughts about a piece. He relished the opportunity to discuss/argue changes or choices and never took anything personally, nor should the author, he believed. He loved working on the journal and was always eager to discuss its potential, frequently sending emails to us about various aspects of the work. His correspondence lay gloriously somewhere between an encyclopedia entry and a slam poem; unique, informed and evocative writing, marrying a mid-west sensibility with a New York City flare. George compiled much of the style manual we use today and so we often have the pleasure of being with his words. 96

William Hurst PHD LP

William Hurst

wjhurstphd@gmail.com

William Hurst   Former philosophy professor, and a psychoanalyst with a private practice in Brooklyn, NY. A graduate of CMPS, he is a training and supervising analyst, and a member of the faculty of CMPS and of BGSP-NY. Since 2020 he has been Editor in Chief of Modern Psychoanalysis. Dr. Hurst is also the former director of the CMPS Extension Division. He has published psychoanalytic and philosophical articles and is the translator of Francoise Davoine's La Folie Wittgenstein—Wittgenstein's Folly (Routledge, 2024).

The author presents a personal/philosophical/psychoanalytic reflection on “leaving,” in this instance on leaving this journal and his position as editor. The philosophical inspiration is Heidegger's work, with an emphasis on the concept of finitude. The roles of thinking, reading, and writing, as well as social engagement are the principal areas of focus. The aim is to inspire others to become more fully engaged in the work of psychoanalysis, not simply as a practice but also as a task always to be taken up— of thinking more deeply and more creatively.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Notes on the Body in Psychoanalysis

Giuseppe Civitarese MD PHD

Giuseppe Civitarese

gcivatarese@gmail.com

Giuseppe Civitarese   Psychiatrist and training and supervising analyst of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society (SPI), a member of the American Psychoanalytic Association (APsaA) and of the International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA). He is in private practice in Pavia, Italy. His most recent books include Sublime Subjects: Aesthetic Experience and Intersubjectivity in Psychoanalysis, London 2018; Vitality and Play in Psychoanalysis (with A. Ferro), Milan 2022; Psychoanalytic Field Theory: A Contemporary Introduction, London 2022; The Hour of Birth: Psychoanalysis of the Sublime and Contemporary Art, London 2023, in press; On Arrogance: A Psychoanalytic Essay, London 2023. In 2022, he received the Sigourney Award.

The author explores the theme of the body in psychoanalysis, focusing on the complex mind/body split and its role in psychic suffering. He argues that this split originates from a strict Superego, often formed when the child does not feel recognized, leading to the creation of a “false self.” This split results in the neglect of bodily needs, with defenses built around rationality, contributing to suffering. The role of the body in psychoanalytic ontology is highlighted, showing how psychic suffering reflects breaks in the emotional fabric connecting individuals. Drawing from Bion's work, the author emphasizes the importance of affect in psychoanalysis, proposing that emotion, deeply tied to bodily experiences, is a key element in meaning-making. The therapeutic task, he therefore asserts, involves reintegrating the psyche with the body by creating a nurturing emotional environment. Finally, the author reflects on the challenges and potentials of teleanalysis, suggesting that while physical presence enhances therapy, the essence of psychoanalysis remains intact even at a distance.

Working with Nullification in the Treatment of Schizoid Personality Disorder

John Madonna MA MA CAGS EdD Cert Psya

John Madonna

Drjmadonna@verizon.net

John Madonna   Licensed psychologist, training analyst, faculty member, supervisor and teacher at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP). He has written and presented papers on the treatment of children, adolescents and adults. He is co-author of The Play Therapy Treatment of Sexually Abused Children, and Treating Police Stress, and he is the author and editor of Emotional Presence in Psychoanalysis: Theory and Clinical Applications.

In discussing the intra and interpersonal needs of those suffering from schizoid personality disorder, the author argues for the need to be perceived, understood and sensitively responded to in order for the psychoanalytic treatment to have optimal effect. He goes on to examine how such patients utilize various behaviors and ways of being which nullify the possibility for emotional contact and the relationship which they desire but dread. The author considers how analysts who are able to live in and tolerate the psychic experience of the patient, resolve their own resistances to contact and utilize emotion to do so, are better able to advance emotional presence and relate more easily.

Frances Bigda-Peyton   Faculty member the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP) and serves as a member of the research committee. Her current interests are in couples’ treatment, integrative medicine that incorporates conventional and Eastern therapies, and eco-psychology—in particular, resistance to making needed structural, cognitive, and affective changes to address climate change.

The author examines the modern analytic treatment of pleasure intolerance in two high-achieving female patients. The study introduces the memory reconsolidation intervention, employed within the analytic framework, as a promising therapeutic technique. This intervention is contrasted with other methods of therapeutic action. Multi-disciplinary literature related to pleasure intolerance is reviewed, highlighting its neurological underpinnings.

responseSet.title: Modern Group Fundamentals: The Role of the Leader
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Modern Group Fundamentals: The Role of the Leader

William Sharp Psya D and Barbara D'Amato Psya D LP

Barbara D'Amato

sharpw@BGSP.edu

drbarbaradamato@gmail.om

Barbara D'Amato   Faculties of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) and the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis at New York (BGSP-NY), where she serves as a clinical supervisor and training analyst. She is director of the CMPS Distance Learning Program. She has been interested in group work since her days as a special education teacher and has written about the group process in psychoanalytic training. She leads ongoing psychoanalytic groups from her private practice in New York City.

The authors explore some aspects of what might go into developing a modern psychoanalytic group therapy leader. Concepts from modern psychoanalysis—-following the contact, progressive communication, and working with initial treatment destructive resistances—are also explored as they relate to leadership. Case examples are used to highlight the work.

Won't Take it Lying Down: A Single Case Study of Couch Resistance

Juan Faraoni PsyaD LMHC LPC

Juan Faraoni

Email: juan@faraonianalytic.com

Juan Faraoni   Clinical supervisor, fellow, professor, and director of the Master of Arts in Clinical Mental Health Counseling program at The Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP). In addition to his academic work, he holds private practices in Hartford, Connecticut and Brookline, Massachusetts. Dr. Faraoni has previously directed several clinical programs in human service organizations serving various communities such as those with physical and mental disabilities, addictions, dual-diagnosis, and the LGBTQ+ community.

This single case study examines the meaning and function of a borderline patient's resistance to the use of the couch throughout an ongoing seven-year analysis. The findings reveal a status quo resistance expressed by a refusal to use the couch. The refusal is understood to be an expression of an unconscious fear/wish of intimacy, which is attached to a fantasy of the patient being hurt and/or the patient having and acting on an impulse to kill. The study includes an exploration of countertransferences and the narcissistic defense.

responseSet.title: Dispelling Illusions of Locality: Panpsychism, Telepathy, Precognition, and Modern Psychoanalysis
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Dispelling Illusions of Locality: Panpsychism, Telepathy, Precognition, and Modern Psychoanalysis

Dan Gilhooley PsyaD LP

Dan Gilhooley

dangilhooley@yahoo.com

Dan Gilhooley   Visual artist and psychoanalyst on the faculties of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP) and the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS). Elected to the National Academy of Design, he has held 18 one-person exhibitions, and in 1995 received NAAP's Gradiva Award for Visual Art contributing to an understanding of psychoanalysis. He has written articles and book chapters on art-making and psychoanalysis, dreaming, intersubjectivity, psi and clinical process. With his patient Frank Toich, Gilhooley published Psychoanalysis, intersubjective writing, and a postmaterialist model of mind: I woke up dead (Routledge) which shared the 2020 Gradiva Award for Outstanding Psychoanalytic Book.

The author uses his experiences from a single case to reconceptualize modern psychoanalysis within a model of what he describes as a “nonlocal mind.” The author argues that the belief in the mind being the product of the brain and residing in the body is an illusion of consciousness. Instead, offering evidence that the unconscious mind is inherently nonlocal, he appropriates William James’ panpsychist transmission theory which claims the mind is a property of nature preexisting our encounter with it. The author reconceptualizes modern psychoanalysis as a nonlocal telepathic process. In reviewing precognition, the author considers evidence from quantum physics and social psychology supporting retrocausation. Examining Huw Price's reconception of quantum entanglement as a retrocausal process, the author notes the similarity of Price's model to the psychoanalytic conception of regression in the service of the ego. Combining Aristotle's teleology with Christopher Bollas’ notion of “destiny drive,” the author proposes we are each motivated by both our past and future.
